Real-time object detectors are usually reported by mean latency o r frame rate. An availability failure,
however, occurs when a single response misses the application' s deadline. Candidate-inflation latency
attacks drive the number of boxes entering non-maximum suppres sion (NMS) far beyond its clean
range. Recent evaluations report that realistic hardware, represen tations and optimized suppression
reduce the severity of such attacks. Reduced severity is not a bo und: work remains attacker-controlled,
and prior studies do not jointly report deadline-relative tail la tency and deadline-miss ratio for a
defended serving path. We therefore admit at most K candidates to NMS. The selection operation
is standard; new is its use as a deployment-selected bound on a ttacker-controlled work, calibrated

Backend choice substantially reduces attacked
suppression latency, but no uncapped backend we
tested satisfies the declared suppression screen.
Following the deployment-realism concern of prior
work [ 15, 16], we replay identical attacked can-
didate arrays through three suppression imple-
mentations. Over the same 48 images the sup-
pression call's p95 is 635.35 ms on the deployed
NumPy path, 177.71 ms on torchvision CPU and
49.08 ms on torchvision CUDA. CPU arms use the
host clock. CUDA arms are bracketed by device
synchronization after a warm-up, since an unsyn-
chronized timing measures the kernel launch, not
the work. The host-to-device copy is excluded; at
0.183 ms p95 it changes neither ordering nor ver-
dict, so the CUDA figure understates a backend
fed from the host.
5

evidence.excerpt:
Top-K selection is a standard operation and we
claim no novelty for it. What is proposed here is its
use as a deployment-selected bound on attacker-
controlled work, with the value calibrated against
a declared deadline and its accuracy cost mea-
sured. Let C be the candidates surviving the
confidence threshold and N = |C|. Before NMS
we retain only CK = TopK( C, K), admitting for
N > K the K candidates smallest under the
lexicographic key ( −sj, j): argpartition on the
negated scores at index K − 1 locates the cutoff,
every candidate strictly above it is admitted, and
the remaining places go to candidates equal to it in
ascending index order. The tie rule is not a formal-
ity, NumPy's introselect being unstable and exact
ties reachable at fp16 or quantized scores. The cut
is O(N ) and adds no pairwise IoU comparison, the
term Eq. ( 4) bounds.
For a serial greedy NMS implementation,

evidence.excerpt:
Figure 3 evaluates several values of K under
three admission policies: the deployed global bud-
get, which admits at most K candidates in total,
and the per-class and per-level alternatives. Only
the global policy makes the admitted total a
declared quantity, so Eq. ( 4) applies to it alone.
The other two are plotted for completeness; equal
labels there are not equal admitted work, and the
curves are not a ranking. The operating point
K = 1024 reduces attacked suppression p95 to
4.28 ms. Its clean cost is the paired difference of
the last two rows of Table 1, 0.00064 AP@[ .50 :
.95], and 0.00060 when the clean evaluation is
replayed through the serving pool. Both are vali-
dation figures, while §3's headline accuracy is held
out, and a cost measured on one population can-
not be subtracted from an accuracy measured on
another; so we repeated the sweep on test-dev
with K fixed

served deadline
The cap reduces client-side p95 under attack by
a factor of 15.10, a median over five independent
A/B sessions, yet the defended requests still miss
De2e = 33 .3 ms every time. That is no contra-
diction: the work bound applies to suppression,
and TNMS ≤ Dsupp does not imply Le2e ≤ De2e.
Nor is the miss attributable to the attack alone.
Attacked images must be delivered losslessly, since
re-encoding at the quality this pool serves did
not preserve the perturbation, so comparing them
against the JPEG corpus varies two things at once.
We therefore re-encoded the same 48 sources into
the attacked arm's format and served all three
arms through the same pool at the same cap, in
ten sessions of 144 requests at ϵ = 2/255.
The adversary turns out not to be necessary for
the miss. Clean lossless images reach p95 66.20 ms
at a deadline-miss ratio of 0.927, against 61.20

evidence.excerpt:
The anchor grid sets the maximum candidate
count, so a cap validated on one output tensor
says little about another. We repeated the capture
and the sweep on the same detector family with-
out its P2 head: 33,600 anchors against 136,000,
a factor of four in the quantity that sets the
ceiling. K = 1024 holds the suppression budget
on both, 3.11 ms against 4.19 ms in the same
run, while the runtime's shipped ceiling of 30,000
misses on both, at 187.30 and 342.96 ms. This is
suppression replay only; no accuracy claim is made
for the second model, and the bound is estab-
lished for the two geometries tested rather than
for anchor-based detectors in general.

evidence.excerpt:
The promoted package is evaluated unchanged on
BDD100K [ 24], a driving corpus whose clean can-
didate distribution is more than an order of mag-
nitude sparser than VisDrone's, while attacked
counts land at much the same level on both.
Their ratio therefore rises to 1777.19, which mea-
sures how little natural load a sparse corpus
carries and is not a severity ranking. The same
K = 1024 defense nonetheless gives a client-side
attacked p95 speedup of 14.04 over 144 requests
per arm, and the cleanest attribution here: BDD's
clean capped deadline-miss ratio is 0.0, so the
attacked 1.0 on the same arm has no floor to sub-
tract. Transfer across input distributions is what
EV ADE found published attacks to lack [ 15]; we
report it for the defense.

missing_information: No reproducible review or selection methodology was detected.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: The final evaluation uses objective wall-clock latency, deadline-miss ratio, and held-out COCO AP metrics measured on the exported serving path, which are independent of the differentiable surrogate used to craft attacks.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Client-scope p95 latency, deadline-miss ratio, and COCO AP@[.50:.95] on held-out test data.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Projected gradient ascent on a differentiable surrogate maximizing the count of candidates passing the confidence threshold before NMS.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: All claims are strictly supported by paired measurements and realistic controls; the authors avoid overclaiming by explicitly showing that the hardened artifact still fails end-to-end deadline requirements due to payload decode overheads, thus proving bounded suppression is necessary but not sufficient.
primary.evaluation_assessment: The empirical evaluation rigorously compares clean and attacked pipelines across datasets (VisDrone2019, BDD100K) and architectures, explicitly separating client, worker, and suppression timing scopes while reporting p95 tail latencies and deadline-miss ratios under thermal throttling and varied payload encodings.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Final evaluation evaluates objective hardware execution times, deadline compliance across distinct backends, and standard mAP metrics on held-out test sets without any shared surrogate loss.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: System-level wall-clock 95th percentile latency, deadline-miss ratio (DMR), and COCO AP@[.50:.95] detection accuracy on held-out test data.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Projected gradient ascent maximizing the count of candidate bounding boxes passing the confidence threshold before NMS.

primary.limitations: The authors transparently report that the defense only bounds stage-specific algorithmic IoU comparisons without guaranteeing hardware worst-case execution time or preventing end-to-end violations caused by upstream bottlenecks like image decompression.
primary.method_assessment: The methodology is thoroughly detailed, describing a deterministic PGD-based candidate inflation attack, a lexicographic Top-K selection rule calibrated against a declared deadline, and stage-isolated latency profiling spanning multiple software backends (NumPy, PyTorch CPU/CUDA) and hardware platforms (RTX 4090 pool and Raspberry Pi 4B).
primary.quality_rationale: The work provides rigorous experimental design, meticulous profiling across independent scopes, transparent negative results regarding full serving pipeline compliance, and thorough ablation across models, datasets, and platforms.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper demonstrates that bounding candidate box admissions prior to non-maximum suppression (NMS) effectively limits attacker-controlled latency inflation in real-time object detection, while precisely quantifying the resulting held-out accuracy loss and showing that post-NMS bottleneck shifts (such as image decoding) prevent stage-level latency bounds from guaranteeing end-to-end deadline integrity.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The work provides rigorous experimental design, meticulous profiling across independent scopes, transparent negative results regarding full serving pipeline compliance, and thorough ablation across models, datasets, and platforms.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The authors transparently report that the defense only bounds stage-specific algorithmic IoU comparisons without guaranteeing hardware worst-case execution time or preventing end-to-end violations caused by upstream bottlenecks like image decompression.

limitations_or_uncertainty.value: Structured research-card claims use title, abstract/summary, metadata, screening rules, and curation. A separate scholarly-quality assessment used bounded full-text excerpts, but unsupported claim, method, or evidence fields remain unextracted.

title: Deadline-Aware Hardening of Real-Time Object Detection Against Candidate-Inflation Latency Attacks
